name: Maia
confidence_why: Hardin 2002, Easton & May 2004 and May & Loeweke 1985 all describe Maia stress as contrastive and carried by the person prefixes (stressed plural 'i-/'ni- against unstressed singular i-/ni-, as in 'isupe 'to us' vs i'supe 'to me'), and they differ only on where stress falls by default in words without such a prefix, which Hardin 2002 puts on the second syllable and May & Loeweke 1985 on the first.

new_statements.quote: p. 11: "4. Stress. In all four languages stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples of contrastive stress are as follows:" — p. 12: "Maia /i'supe/ 'to me' /'isupe/ 'to us' /ni'buae/ 'your father' /'nibuae/ 'all you fathers'. An interesting feature of stress has been noted in comparing two syllable words that are similar in all four languages. Maia tends to stress the first syllable, whereas Maiani, Miani and Mala stress the second syllable. /'arop/ 'three' (Maia) /a'rop/ 'three' (Maiani, Miani) /nga'rop/ 'three' (Mala) /'ulum/ 'dirty' (Maia) /u'lum/ 'dirty' (Maiani, Mala) /u'rum/ 'dirty' (Miani)" — p. 13: "Stress - - - not written - - -" and "5.3 None of the men write stress as it makes the words look too different from English or Tok Pisin."

Maia data here = Saki (inland Maia), examples from Morris Lolomir and Jacob Muain; Pila (coastal Maia) is explicitly not covered.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic) in Maia as in its three sister languages; the Maia minimal pairs oppose a stressed plural prefix ('isupe 'to us', 'nibuae 'all you fathers') to an unstressed singular prefix with stress on the following syllable (i'supe 'to me', ni'buae 'your father'). In disyllabic words Maia tends to stress the first syllable where Maiani, Miani and Mala stress the second ('arop 'three', 'ulum 'dirty'). Stress is not written in the recommended orthography.
new_statements.exceptions: Only a tendency is stated for disyllables; the contrastive pairs are all singular vs plural prefix contrasts. §2.4.2 (p. 6) notes the vibrant is a flap between vowels in unstressed syllables. p. 13-14: writers proposed marking stress with h or a doubled consonant, neither adopted.
new_statements.identity_note: May & Loeweke 1985 cover Saki = Maia of the inland villages (examples from Morris Lolomir and Jacob Muain) and explicitly exclude Pila = coastal Maia; Easton & May's OPD is labelled 'Maia (Saki, Inland Maia) Language (Main Dialect)'; the 2008 dictionary states its data represent the central dialect (Wagedav, Urumarav, Turupav). All are the same SIL programme and the same inland/central variety.

new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length). Stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples are as follows: 'isupe 'bring us' / 'nibuae 'your (pl) fathers' / i'supe 'bring me' / ni'buae 'your (sg) father'. In some environments this is realized as length due to morphophonemic changes. 'i:kum 'our heads' / 'ni:pi 'your (pl) tongues' / 'ikum 'my head' / 'nipi 'your (sg) tongue'. [...] Conventions: Orthographic. Phonemic stress is written using double vowels. 'isupe <iisupe> 'bring us' [...] i'supe <isupe> 'bring me'. When this is realized as a lengthened vowel, it is likewise written as a double vowel.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive/phonemic; the contrasts given are stressed plural prefix vs unstressed singular prefix (stress then on the next syllable); in some environments the contrast surfaces as vowel length; the practical orthography writes the stressed/lengthened prefix vowel double (iisupe vs isupe).

new_statements.quote: p. 71: "Stress is normally on the second syllable. But, whenever a 1st or 2nd person plural is used, it is the prefix or first syllable that receives the primary stress. Whenever there is ambiguity and in order to clearly differentiate between first and second person singular and plural, the people have chosen to write the stressed plural prefix with a double vowel. In cases where there is no ambiguity, the single vowel is used." — p. 13: "For 1st and 2nd person, singular and plural differentiated by stress. [...] i- 1st person singular /i'dia/ <idia> 'my skin' [...] 'ni- 2nd person plural /'nidia/ <niidia> 'your (pl) skin' [...] The stress patterns are instrumental in explaining the morphophonemic processes."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the second syllable; the 1st/2nd person plural prefixes (ii-, nii-) are inherently stressed, so with them stress falls on the first syllable, and this is the only place stress distinguishes words (singular vs plural possessor/object). Compound verbs carry one stress; the clitic =na takes no extra stress; imperatives may put more force on the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: 1st/2nd plural prefixes attract primary stress to the first syllable; the placement statement is made in the section on pronoun prefixes and may be meant for prefixed verbs/nouns rather than the whole lexicon.
new_statements.identity_note: May & Loeweke 1985 cover Saki = Maia of the inland villages (examples from Morris Lolomir and Jacob Muain) and explicitly exclude Pila = coastal Maia; Easton & May's OPD is labelled 'Maia (Saki, Inland Maia) Language (Main Dialect)'; the 2008 dictionary states its data represent the central dialect (Wagedav, Urumarav, Turupav). All are the same SIL programme and the same inland/central variety.

readall_conflicts: All three SIL descriptions agree that Maia stress is contrastive/phonemic and that the contrast is carried by the 1st/2nd person plural prefixes (stressed 'i-/'ni- vs unstressed singular i-/ni- with stress on the next syllable: 'isupe vs i'supe, 'nibuae vs ni'buae). They differ on the default position: May & Loeweke 1985 (p. 12) say that in disyllabic words Maia tends to stress the first syllable ('arop 'three', 'ulum 'dirty') where the sister languages stress the second, whereas Hardin 2002 (p. 71, in the section on pronoun prefixes) says stress is normally on the second syllable with the plural prefix pulling it to the first. Hardin's statement may be scoped to prefixed forms; neither source gives a general survey of the lexicon, so the default is not settled. The dictionary is silent.
